Definition: Percentage of the national population covered by at least one 4G/LTE mobile network signal, whether or not they subscribe to the service. 4G is the practical minimum for meaningful broadband connectivity enabling digital services.
redteam_note: Only one source for a substantive score — corroborate.
revision_notes: Confirmed. POTRAZ's own 2024 Annual Sector Report (primary regulator source) records total LTE population coverage of 51.6% in 2024 (up from 44.7% in 2023), consistent with the 50% figure cited for 2021. Both fall in the 50-74% band, so Value Code 3 stands; source updated to the more authoritative and current POTRAZ regulator report.

Definition: Percentage of individuals who used the internet (from any location, via any device) in the last three months. This measures actual internet adoption beyond network availability, capturing the combined effect of infrastructure, affordability, digital literacy, and relevance.

revision_notes: Confirmed. DataReportal/Kepios put internet penetration at 38.4% (end 2025); Internet Society Pulse independently reports 42% (2024, vs 40% Africa average). Both corroborating sources fall in the 30-49% band, so Value Code 3 is confirmed.

Definition: Unique mobile subscriber penetration rate as a percentage of the total population. Measures the proportion of individuals who subscribe to a mobile service (not SIM cards, which can be multiple per person). Mobile phones are the primary device for internet access in Africa.
redteam_note: Only one source for a substantive score — corroborate.
revision_notes: Confirmed with caveat. POTRAZ reports mobile SUBSCRIPTION penetration of 102-107% (2024-2025, multi-SIM inclusive) and GSMA/DataReportal shows 95-107% connections/population. Neither is a true unique-subscriber figure, but even after a typical multi-SIM adjustment (~1.3x in this market) unique penetration plausibly still exceeds 70%, supporting Value Code 5. Note for human review: no source gives a true GSMA unique-subscriber percentage for Zimbabwe.

revision_notes: NOT CONFIRMED — human review recommended. The cited GSMA Mobile Economy Sub-Saharan Africa report gives a regional (SSA-wide) smartphone adoption range, not a Zimbabwe-specific figure. Targeted searches for a POTRAZ or GSMA Intelligence country-level smartphone percentage did not return a definitive figure before search capacity was exhausted. Value Code 4 is plausible (POTRAZ narrative confirms rising smartphone penetration and ISOC Pulse shows 49% of population with 4G-capable device access) but is not verified against an authoritative Zimbabwe-specific statistic. Recommend a follow-up search of GSMA Intelligence country data or POTRAZ quarterly reports for an explicit percentage.

Definition: Whether the country has enacted comprehensive data protection and privacy legislation. A foundational legal requirement for building trust in digital public infrastructure and for enabling secure cross-border data flows under frameworks like the AU Convention on Cyber Security and Personal Data Protection.
Value Name: Legislation enacted with Data Protection Authority established
Comments: Cyber and Data Protection Act enacted, POTRAZ DPA. [Michalsons](https://www.michalsons.com/blog/zimbabwes-cyber-and-data-protection-act-overview/78795)
redteam_note: Only one source for a substantive score — corroborate.
revision_notes: Confirmed and strengthened. Cyber and Data Protection Act [Chapter 12:07] (2021) explicitly designates POTRAZ as the Data Protection Authority, and SI 155 of 2024 (licensing of data controllers/DPOs, in force with a March 2025 compliance deadline) demonstrates active enforcement machinery. Multiple independent legal sources (DLA Piper, Michalsons, MawereSibanda) corroborate. Value Code 4 confirmed; a case could be made for 5 given active licensing enforcement, but regional alignment evidence is insufficient, so kept conservative at 4.

Definition: The presence and tier quality of commercial/colocation data center facilities operating in the country. Commercial data centers provide the physical infrastructure for hosting cloud services, content delivery, and enterprise applications domestically.
redteam_note: Only one source for a substantive score — corroborate.
revision_notes: Score raised from 2 to 3. Since the original Cloudscene citation (TelOne, small-scale), Africa Data Centres (the continent's Tier III operator in Johannesburg, Lagos and Nairobi) and Econet jointly commissioned a 5MW commercial data centre in Harare (June 2025) with redundant power, multi-carrier connectivity and hyperscaler partnerships (Google, Microsoft) — a materially higher-grade facility than Tier I-II. Formal Tier III certification was not confirmed in available sources (Exa search credits exhausted), so flagged for human confirmation of exact tier rating, but the evidence supports at least one Tier III-equivalent facility (Value Code 3) rather than small-scale only.

Value Name: National data center operational with cloud strategy adopted
Comments: Operational cloud strategy, Tier IV data centers, public digital infra in AI Strategy. [Zim AI Strategy](https://veritaszim.net/sites/veritas_d/files/Zimbabwe%20National%20Artificial%20Intelligence%20Strategy.pdf)
redteam_note: Only one source for a substantive score — corroborate.
revision_notes: Confirmed with better sources. Zimbabwe's National Data Centre has been operational since 2021 (built with Chinese government/Inspur Group support, serving all ministries via cloud computing), per an independent e-governance analysis. In May 2026 the ICT Minister formally announced a 'Zimbabwe Government Cloud' policy and Government Service Bus, consolidating the cloud strategy referenced in the Smart Zimbabwe 2030 Master Plan. This confirms Value Code 4 (operational data centre plus adopted cloud strategy) on stronger evidence than the original AI Strategy PDF citation, which did not itself substantiate the claim.

Definition: Percentage of national population with access to electricity (grid or off-grid). This is the primary indicator of energy infrastructure availability for ICT. Based on World Bank/IEA Tracking SDG7 data, national statistical offices, or Afrobarometer surveys.
redteam_note: Only one source for a substantive score — corroborate.
revision_notes: Confirmed with fresher figure. World Bank data (EG.ELC.ACCS.ZS) shows access to electricity rose to 62.0% in 2023 (from 50.1% in 2022), well above the 52.75% (2020) figure originally cited. Both old and new figures fall in the 50-74% band, so Value Code 3 is confirmed; comments/source updated to the current 2023 World Bank figure.

Definition: Whether the country has established policies, regulations, and programmes supporting off-grid and distributed energy solutions (mini-grids, solar home systems). These are critical for extending ICT infrastructure to unserved areas beyond the central grid.
redteam_note: Only one source for a substantive score — corroborate.
revision_notes: Confirmed with better sources (original GOGLA link is dead). Zimbabwe has a National Renewable Energy Policy (2019, ZERA) and Rural Electrification Fund Act providing the policy framework; the government has since developed a dedicated mini-grid policy framework (with GCIEP, 2026) and launched Zimbabwe's first Renewable Energy Fund (REF Zimbabwe, Sept 2024, with UNCDF/UNESCO/UNDP/UN Women) targeting mini-grids and stand-alone solar in underserved areas. This is 'active policy with some deployment' (Value Code 3) rather than a mature, widely-deployed framework, so the code is confirmed.

Definition: The gap between urban and rural electricity access rates. A smaller gap indicates more equitable energy distribution, critical for ensuring ICT infrastructure can serve the whole population, not just cities.
redteam_note: Only one source for a substantive score — corroborate.
revision_notes: Score changed from 2 to 3. Fresher World Bank data (EG.ELC.ACCS.RU.ZS / URB.ZS) shows urban access at 84% and rural access at 51.4% in 2023 — a gap of 32.6 percentage points, versus the 48pp gap implied by the 2020 figures originally cited. This narrower, more current gap falls in the 21-40pp band (Value Code 3), not 41-60pp. The rural figure is also consistent with the national 62% access rate reported for 2023 given Zimbabwe's urban/rural population split, giving confidence in the correction.

Definition: The size and vibrancy of the local software developer and technology professional community. Measured through proxies such as GitHub activity, Stack Overflow representation, local tech meetup groups, and developer surveys. Indicates the country's capacity to build and maintain digital systems locally.
redteam_note: Only one source for a substantive score — corroborate.
revision_notes: Confirmed with a broader proxy. Community-maintained GitHub trackers (Nov 2025) count 918-921 Zimbabwe-linked GitHub users with at least 2 followers — a much larger and more representative sample than Gitista's list of 39 high-follower (50+) contributors. Given that GitHub-visible developers with public profiles are only a subset of the true developer population, this is consistent with an active, 'Developing' community in the 1,000-10,000 range (Value Code 3), though no single authoritative census of total developers exists — treat as a reasonable estimate rather than a precise count.

Definition: The country's e-government development level based on the UN E-Government Development Index (EGDI). This composite index measures online service delivery, telecommunications infrastructure, and human capital. Indicates the government's capacity to deliver digital public services.
redteam_note: Only one source for a substantive score — corroborate.
revision_notes: Score corrected from 3 to 2. The original row's own comment flagged the inconsistency (EGDI 0.4717 falls in the Middle band, yet Value Code 3 = High 0.50-0.64 was recorded — a scoring error). Verified directly against the UN EGOVKB database: Zimbabwe's 2024 EGDI is 0.4481 (rank 149 of 193), which the ICT Minister herself has publicly confirmed as 'Middle' band. Per the metadata scale (0.25-0.49 = Middle = Code 2), this is Code 2, not Code 3. Corrected on three independent, directly-verified sources.

Definition: The gap between men and women in mobile internet usage or internet access. Based on the GSMA Mobile Gender Gap data or ITU gender-disaggregated ICT statistics. A smaller gap indicates more equitable access to digital opportunities.
redteam_note: Only one source for a substantive score — corroborate.
revision_notes: FLAGGED FOR HUMAN REVIEW — not confirmed, and original score is unsupported. The cited source measures the Sub-Saharan Africa REGIONAL gender gap (29% for mobile internet, GSMA 2025 report); it is not Zimbabwe-specific evidence and Zimbabwe is not among the countries surveyed in the GSMA Mobile Gender Gap Report. A Zimbabwe-specific source (Internet Society Pulse) instead shows internet use by gender at Female 30% / Male 29% — implying near parity, not a large gap — but this is a single aggregator source of unclear underlying methodology. Given the conflict between a mismatched regional figure and an unverified country-specific one, the code is set to 0 (evidence genuinely unclear) pending human review and a search for authoritative Zimbabwe-specific ITU or GSMA country data.
